title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. This is the final paragraph of E443. A free–free elastic lamina AB is pinned by a stylus at an interior point C. The deflection on each side of C is written as A cos(θx/b) + B sin(θx/b) + C e^{θx/b} + D e^{−θx/b}, with primed constants on the other side. The previous page treats the symmetric case where C is the midpoint (β = α). There ζ = ζ' = θα/b, with α the half-length. The free-end conditions give C = DV and C' = D'V, where V = (−cos ζ + sin ζ − e^{−ζ})/(cos ζ + sin ζ + e^{ζ}). The two matching conditions at C (the seventh and eighth equations) factor into (D − D')·[...] = 0 and (D + D')·[...] = 0. So either D' = −D or D' = D.

Case I (D' = −D). The condition is (V+1) sin ζ − (V−1) cos ζ − V e^ζ + e^{−ζ} = 0. Solving for V gives V = (s + c + e^{−ζ})/(c − s + e^{ζ}). Equating this to the free-end value of V and using (c+s)² + (c−s)² = 2, everything collapses to 4 + 2 cos ζ (e^ζ + e^{−ζ}) = 0. That is Euler's 2 = −cos ζ (e^ζ + e^{−ζ}), i.e. cos ζ cosh ζ = −1. This is the clamped–free (cantilever) frequency equation for one half of the bar. The modes are those in which the slope vanishes at the pin, so each half behaves as a cantilever of length α. Hence Euler's remark that the bar vibrates 'as in our principal evolution' (the wall-clamped lamina) with the length halved. Roots: ζ ≈ 1.8751, 4.6941, ...

Case II (D' = D). The condition (V+1) cos ζ + (V−1) sin ζ − V e^ζ − e^{−ζ} = 0 gives V = (s − c + e^{−ζ})/(c + s − e^{ζ}). Equating to the free-end value yields (cos ζ − sin ζ) e^ζ = (cos ζ + sin ζ) e^{−ζ}. That is Euler's e^{2ζ} = (cos ζ + sin ζ)/(cos ζ − sin ζ), equivalently tanh ζ = tan ζ. This is the pinned–free frequency equation for each half: the moment vanishes at the pin, so these are the modes antisymmetric in the transverse displacement. Euler identifies this with his Problem II (lamina fixed by a stylus at one end, free at the other) for half the length. Roots: ζ = 0 (rigid rotation about the pin, not a vibration), then ≈ 3.9266, 7.0686, ...

Euler closes by saying it is now easy to see how to set up the calculation if the lamina were pinned at several points. In modern terms that is the multi-span continuous-beam vibration problem.
errors: No algebraic errors: both reductions (cos ζ cosh ζ = −1 and e^{2ζ} = (cos+sin)/(cos−sin) ⇔ tan ζ = tanh ζ) check out exactly.
Gap: the case II equation admits the trivial root ζ = 0, which corresponds to rigid rotation about the pin, not a vibration. It is not mentioned on this page.

Which sign of D'/D corresponds to the symmetric or antisymmetric mode depends on Euler's coordinate convention (abscissae presumably measured from each free end toward C). The physical identification stated in the text (cantilever versus pinned–free) is nonetheless correct.

ideas.what: For a free–free beam pinned at its midpoint, the modes split into two families equivalent to half-length clamped–free and half-length pinned–free beams.
ideas.modern_name: Symmetry (even/odd) decomposition of beam modes; reduction of a symmetric two-span beam to half-span problems
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard textbook result (Rayleigh, Theory of Sound, and later vibration texts); Euler's earlier beam vibration work (E40, Commentarii 1735/1740) gave the cantilever case
ideas.where_published: E443 itself, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 17 (1772/1773); discussed in Truesdell's Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Frequency equation for the cantilever, cos ζ cosh ζ = −1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E40 and later papers); Daniel Bernoulli
ideas.where_published: E40 and the 'principal evolution' of E443

ideas.what: Frequency equation for the pinned–free beam, tan ζ = tanh ζ
Remark that the method extends to a lamina pinned at several points
ideas.modern_name: Vibrations of continuous multi-span beams (later handled by Clapeyron's three-moment equations and transfer-matrix methods)
ideas.where_published: Only as a remark here; I do not know of a separate Euler treatment

deep.surprise_reason: The page completes a routine symmetric-case reduction whose result (half-length cantilever modes and half-length pinned–free modes) is standard. E443 is well covered by Truesdell. The closing remark about multiple pins is only a suggestion, and the multi-span problem was fully developed later; nothing here appears absent from the record.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially faithful. 'cos ζ' in case II lacks the dot in the print ('cof ζ'), which is immaterial.
On the previous page, 'V+1.sin.ζ' should be read as '(V+1) sin ζ'.
